title: The Storm Inside the Snow Globe

segments.text: [soft, slow, warm voice] [softly] Settle somewhere safe and bring to mind an urge that is workable, not overwhelming. Imagine holding a snow globe without needing to shake or steady it.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Name the urge simply: wanting... checking... escaping... reaching. A name is a label on the glass, not an instruction.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Locate its strongest body sensation. Perhaps pressure, heat, restlessness, tightness, or a bright electric pull.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Imagine those sensations as snow moving inside the globe. Notice speed, density, direction, and where the storm is most active.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Let the breath remain natural. You are not blowing the snow away; you are staying present while gravity does its quiet work.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Rate the urge gently from zero to ten, then become curious about whether the number stays perfectly still.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Watch for a crest, a dip, or a change of texture. Even an urge that remains strong is changing in tiny ways.
[soft, slow, warm voice] [reassuringly] You can choose distance from the trigger, ask for support, or leave the situation. Surfing an urge does not mean refusing practical help.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Picture more flakes settling onto a miniature town. Windows reappear. Streets return. The storm was real, and it was also temporary weather.
[soft, slow, warm voice] Choose one next action that serves you better than the urge: wait five minutes, drink water, move rooms, message someone, or simply keep breathing.
[soft, slow, warm voice] [softly] Put the snow globe down in imagination. Feel your real hands and remember: a signal may be loud without becoming your commander.
